label: A
text: Japan has long been associated with disciplined saving, meticulous craft, and a quiet confidence in long-term planning. Economists who study household behavior often point to cultural habits formed across generations: families treat surplus income as a buffer against uncertainty, not as fuel for impulsive consumption. That instinct shaped everything from postal savings accounts to the popularity of low-risk government bonds.

label: B
text: In the decades after the Second World War, this thrift became an engine of national recovery. Capital that might have leaked into luxury markets instead financed factories, rail networks, and export industries. The phrase “land of the rising sum” was coined by a foreign correspondent who noticed how ordinary deposits, multiplied by millions of households, quietly rebuilt a modern economy.

label: C
text: Yet the same habits later created new tensions. When interest rates fell and asset prices stalled, households kept saving while firms hesitated to invest. Policymakers struggled to convert private caution into public growth. Critics argued that a culture celebrated for prudence had become an obstacle to demand, innovation, and risk-taking among younger workers.

label: D
text: Today, fintech apps, side hustles, and global investment products are rewriting the story again. Young adults still value security, but they also chase yield through index funds and overseas markets. The old moral of patient accumulation has not disappeared—it has simply learned to travel digitally, seeking opportunity beyond domestic borders.
